label: Cayley-Klein Geometries at Work
notes: This chapter, printed pages 423 to 442, turns the Cayley-Klein framework into a calculator. One absolute conic, a few cross-ratios, and the same matrix algebra deliver distances, angles, perpendiculars and circles in elliptic, Euclidean, hyperbolic and relativistic geometry. The slogan: change the absolute, keep the machinery.

label: One Machine, Many Geometries
notes: Recall the single recipe. Points and lines are homogeneous vectors, the absolute is a symmetric matrix A with dual B, and every measurement is a cross-ratio against the absolute. Distances use the primal conic, angles use the dual conic. Walk through how this one apparatus specializes by tuning A.

label: The Absolute Dictionary
notes: Present the dictionary that drives the whole deck. Each geometry is just a choice of signature for the absolute. Elliptic is definite, hyperbolic is the real disk, Euclidean and Galilean are degenerate, Minkowski has a real light cone. Emphasize that the same formulas run; only the matrix entries differ.

label: Distance From the Absolute
notes: Derive the distance measurement. The line through two points meets the absolute in two fundamental points; the cross-ratio of the four points, fed through a logarithm, gives distance. Show how the elliptic, hyperbolic and Euclidean constants emerge from the same cross-ratio as the absolute changes.

label: Orthogonality Is Pole-Polar
notes: This is the chapter's keystone. A right angle is not Euclidean intuition but the algebraic test l-transpose B m equals zero. When Bl is nonzero it is the pole of l, so the perpendicular to l through p is the join of p with Bl. Stress the constructive flavor.

label: Altitudes: Constructive vs Implicit
notes: Warn students about two versions of every theorem. The constructive altitude joins a vertex to a genuine pole and concurs reliably. The implicit version only asks for a line satisfying the bilinear equation, and when B drops to rank one those equations stop constraining anything. Degeneracy breaks the implicit theorem.

label: Same Test, Different Pictures
notes: The one equation l-transpose B m equals zero shows three faces. Euclidean eyes see slopes multiplying to minus one. The pseudo-Euclidean absolute reflects slopes across the diagonal so orthogonal lines have inverse slopes. In the hyperbolic Klein disk a regular pentagon can have five right angles. Same algebra, different geometry.

label: Midpoints and Bisectors Are Dual
notes: Midpoints and angle bisectors are the same square-root construction, one on points, one on lines. Each delivers a pair, not a single object, and the pair is harmonic with cross-ratio minus one. In the Euclidean limit one midpoint slides to the point at infinity. Highlight the primal-dual symmetry.

label: Trigonometry as a Projective Identity
notes: The law of sines is one projective statement. Build the Psi and Psi-star ratios from the primal and dual conics, take their quotient on each side, and the three quotients agree. The Euclidean, elliptic and hyperbolic sine laws are just specializations obtained by fixing the absolute.

label: Minkowski: The Light Cone Absolute
notes: Relativistic geometry is Cayley-Klein with the light cone as absolute. The cross-ratio measure of angle between timelike directions becomes rapidity, a hyperbolic angle that adds. Velocity addition is rapidity addition; the cone is the unreachable absolute. Connect this to the hyperbolic-distance picture from earlier slides.

label: Translating a Theorem
notes: Demonstrate the translation discipline. Write a theorem once in pole-polar language, then read off its elliptic, Euclidean and hyperbolic instances by swapping the absolute. The projective construction is invariant; only the metric reading changes. This is the payoff of the unified machinery.

label: Recap and Cautions
notes: Close by consolidating. Orthogonality is pole-polar, midpoints and bisectors are dual pairs, the sine law is a Psi ratio identity, and Minkowski geometry fits the same mold with rapidity as angle. Prefer constructive theorems; watch degenerate absolutes where implicit equations lose their grip.
